q: Inside Fronsac sits a smaller appellation drawn around two limestone hills above the Dordogne. Name that inner appellation.
exp: It covers the slopes of the Canon and Saint-Michel hills, where molasse and limestone replace the sandier ground of Fronsac proper. Any grower in Canon-Fronsac may declassify to Fronsac; the reverse is not possible, which is the practical test of which sits above the other.

q: Looking across the estuary at the Medoc, one Right Bank cotes appellation has kept a real planting of a red variety now scarce elsewhere in Bordeaux. Which variety?
exp: Cotes de Bourg is the one place in the region where the grape is still treated as a serious blending component rather than a relic. Its early budding and poor fruit set are why the rest of Bordeaux replanted to Merlot after the 1956 frost.

q: North of the Barbanne lies an appellation of its own that absorbed the neighbouring commune of Neac and is often sold as a cheaper route to Merlot on clay. Name it.
exp: Neac had its own appellation until it was merged in, and the eastern part of the zone on gravel over clay is the part that most resembles Pomerol itself. The western half is sandier and gives the lighter wines that set the price expectation for the whole name.

q: Rounded stones the size of a fist lie metres deep across the best Medoc vineyards. How did they get there?
opts: They weathered in place out of the limestone bedrock under the vineyards
Rivers carried them down from the Pyrenees and the Massif Central
They were dredged from the estuary and spread on the fields by growers
They blew inland as gravel from the Atlantic dunes
exp: The stones came from the Pyrenees and the Massif Central during the Ice Ages: glacial meltwater moved enormous volumes of them north along the Garonne and dumped them in terraces as the flow slackened. The stones are therefore foreign to the Medoc, which is why the ground changes character the moment you step off a terrace.

q: Two Saint-Emilion estates lie a kilometre apart, one at the edge of the limestone plateau and one on sand at the foot of the slope. What difference in the wines should you predict?
opts: The plateau gives sweeter wine because limestone raises sugar
The plateau gives the firmer, longer-lived wine
The sand gives the more tannic and longer-lived wine of the two
There is no reliable difference, since both are planted to Merlot
exp: Limestone holds a water reserve and keeps acidity, so the plateau wines have structure and a long life. The sandy foot of the cotes warms fast and drains hard, giving perfumed, supple wine that is ready early and does not repay cellaring.

q: Under the Pomerol plateau runs a pan of iron-cemented sand, usually called crasse de fer. Growers also give it a blacksmith's name. What is that second term?
exp: Machefer is the word for forge clinker, which is what the stuff looks like when a trench cuts through it. The pan slows drainage, so the vine still has water in a dry August, and growers have long credited it with the iron, truffled note of the best of the plateau.

q: Saint-Emilion's plateau is quarried for building stone as well as planted with vines, and its limestone carries a name taken from the fossils in it. Name that limestone.
exp: The asteries are fragments of fossil starfish left in an Oligocene marine deposit. The same rock was cut out from beneath the town for the buildings above it, which is why the plateau is riddled with cellars at a constant temperature.

q: Before the seventeenth century the Medoc was largely marsh, and foreign engineers were brought in to drain it and expose the gravel. Which country did they come from?
exp: Dutch drainage work is the reason the Medoc has a wine industry at all, and their trade is also why so much early Medoc wine went north rather than to Paris. The drainage channels they cut are still called jalles and still do the job.

q: Deep gravel gives a vine no water reserve to speak of, and in a fine year that shortage is a virtue rather than a problem. What is the term for the mild, controlled version of it?
exp: A vine denied water at veraison stops making leaves and puts its effort into ripening the fruit, which concentrates the berry and thickens the skin. Push it further and the vine shuts down altogether, which is why the same gravel that makes a great dry vintage makes a hard one in drought.

q: Six new varieties were admitted to the Bordeaux and Bordeaux Superieur appellations in 2021 as an adaptation to a warming climate. What limits came with them?
opts: No limit on planting, but no more than twenty percent of the blend
They may be used for rose and clairet only
They may be used in second wines only
Five percent of the planted area, ten percent of the blend
exp: Those figures are ceilings rather than targets, and they are what make the change conservative: the varieties are there to be trialled, not to remake the blend. They are also confined to the two regional appellations, so a communal wine such as Pauillac or Margaux may not use them at all.

q: Beyond Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon and Muscadelle, a white Bordeaux may carry a minority of three older accessory varieties. Which trio?
opts: Colombard, Ugni Blanc and Merlot Blanc
Riesling, Aligote and Melon de Bourgogne
Petit Manseng, Gros Manseng and Courbu
Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc and Viognier
exp: They are capped at a minority share and are mostly a legacy of the distilling and bulk trade, since Colombard and Ugni Blanc are the Cognac grapes. Merlot Blanc really is a child of Merlot, a natural crossing with Folle Blanche found in the Gironde in 1891, and it is now nearly gone.

q: Carmenere remains a permitted Bordeaux red and is almost never seen there. What drove it out?
opts: DNA work showed it to be Merlot under another name
The 1855 brokers struck it from the classified estates
Its wines were barred from export by the negociants
It ripens very late and sets its crop badly
exp: Coulure and late ripening made it unreliable in a maritime climate, it grafted poorly, and replanting after phylloxera was the moment growers dropped it. It went to Chile before all this, where it was long mistaken for Merlot, and it ripens there in a way it rarely did at home.

q: A pink-skinned mutation of Sauvignon Blanc is permitted for white Bordeaux and valued for the weight and stone-fruit character it adds. Name it.
exp: It gives lower acidity and a broader palate than Sauvignon Blanc, so it is used the way Semillon is, to fill out the middle. Several Pessac-Leognan whites carry a few percent of it and never mention it on the label.

q: Bordeaux growers have an old local name for Malbec, still used in the Medoc and quite different from the one used on the Right Bank. What is the Medoc name?
accept: cot the medoc name for malbec
exp: Pressac is the Right Bank name, said to come from the family that spread the vine around Saint-Emilion, and Auxerrois is what the same grape is called in Cahors. One variety with four names is a standard trap on a blind tasting sheet.

q: Around Saint-Emilion, Cabernet Franc goes by a local name that older growers still use in conversation. What is that name?
exp: Cheval Blanc's plantings were traditionally described in those terms, and the same grape is Breton in the Loire. Petit Bouchet is the local name for Cabernet Sauvignon, so the qualifier carries the whole of the difference, and knowing it is what separates following a Right Bank grower's description of a blend from guessing at it.

q: Cellar hands walk the rows of barriques every week or two with a jug, filling each one back up to the bung. Which operation is this?
opts: Collage
Soutirage
Ouillage
Assemblage
exp: Wine evaporates through the staves, and the space left behind would let the wine oxidise and acetify. Topping up keeps the barrel brim full, which is why a traditional cellar is measured in labour as much as in oak.
